abstract: "Increasingly frequent winter warming events cause the environment to alternate from freezing to melting which can have a major impact on lake ecosystems. Specifically, road salt application followed by melting leads to runoff and increased salinity in freshwater ecosystems with detrimental effects on zooplankton communities such as reduction in thermal tolerance. Stressors of high salinity may occur in an isolated manner or in tandem with warming events. Previous work from our lab demonstrated the negative impacts of road salt on copepod survivorship, however, the same negative effects were not observed with artificial sea water. This project seeks to test the effects of major ions found in road salt, NaCl and MgCl2, on survival and thermal limits in two freshwater copepod species, Leptodiaptomus minutus and L. sicilis, with additional survivorship measured in Skistodiaptomus spp.. Copepods were exposed to 8 doses of each salt during a 5-day survivorship experiment followed by critical thermal maximum (CTmax) assays. We observed differences in survivorship between each of the species and treatments. L. sicilis were the most resilient to increased salt concentration followed by L. minutus and Skistodiaptomus spp.. L. minutus is present in the lake from August to January while L. sicilis is present in the lake from November to June, and Skistodiaptomus spp. are present from June to October. These temporal differences in conjunction with ecological history data may describe these trends. Following salt acclimation, thermal limit measurements demonstrated no significant effect of salt exposure on L. minutus thermal limits, however, salt exposure significantly decreased thermal limits in L. sicilis. In today's climate, increasing salt and temperature exist as concurrent environmental stressors. There has been limited work done to understand the relationship of these stressors on freshwater copepods. This work aims to fill that gap to help inform policy and management to protect our lake ecosystem."

# Introduction

Freshwater lake conservation has emerged as a growing concern due to human and climate change driven stressors (Cunillera-Montcusí et al., 2022; O'Reilly et al., 2015) such as increasing salinization (Kaushal et al., 2021; Dugan et al., 2017). Increased salinity has the potential to change the ecosystem services provided by lake systems due to its importance in adaptation, speciation, and community structure (Cunillera-Montcusí et al., 2022; Medina et al., 2007). During periods of melting, runoff can occur into streams, lakes, and wetlands bringing with it excess salt from nearby roads (Kaushal et al. 2005). The increase in salinity can compromise ecosystems and cause mortality in sensitive populations (Melles et al., 2023; Petranka & Doyle 2010). 

Climate induced warming of aquatic systems can disrupt population structures and lead to shifts in phenology, geography, and body size (Ratnarajah et al., 2023). Temperature sensitivities within species are closely related to their phenology with responses in zooplankton moving more quickly than in other animals (Winder et al., 2009; Thackeray et al., 2016; Cooley et al., 2022). Climate related stressors such as temperature increases and a higher abundance of acute warming events (US Environmental Protection Agency, 2021) in the winter coincide with an increase in salinity enhancing a need for further understanding in concurrence of environmental stressors. While these acute events are linked, both increased salinity and temperature individually have detrimental effects on zooplankton communities (Schuler et al. 2017; Winder et al., 2009).

Zooplankton communities are especially sensitive to changes in salinity (Schuler et al. 2017) and are exposed to thermal stress as climate change continues to impact lake ecosystems. The understanding of salinity in freshwater systems has been historically grounded in chloride content. Further work has found that toxicity does differ between ions, but much of this work remains rooted in sodium and chloride levels (Cañ-Argüelles 2020). Salt stress has also been observed to increase cyanobacteria abundance at levels even below local guidelines (McClymont et al., 2023).

An observation in cross tolerance of heat and salt stress in zooplankton and phytoplankton found that where warming elicited a smaller response, higher salt concentrations reduced biomass and richness of zooplankton communities (McClymont et al., 2023). Similar studies have found microevolutionary adaptation to one salt increases the tolerance of species to certain other salts (Zhao et al., 2023). Findings from this study examined how prior NaCl exposure impacted tolerance to other ions (Zhao et al., 2023) highlighting the importance of ion-specific effects within saline stress. Additionally, tolerance to heat and salt individually have demonstrated high impacts on copepod nauplii within a zooplankton mesocosm (Sun & Arnott, 2022). Through the coupling of salt and heat stress, zooplankton communities exhibit losses in biomass and abundance (Sun & Arnott, 2022). Studies on marine copepod cross tolerance have determined a co-variance between temperature and salinity suggesting that as salinity increases, thermal tolerance increases (Denny & Dowd, 2022), limited work has been performed on freshwater copepods. An understanding of the interaction of multiple stressors provides a more complete view of ecosystem responses, but environmental variation remains unpredictable (Dowd et al., 2015).

In field systems, organisms must respond to an abundance of environmental stressors at the same time, and copepods (Calanoida) serve as a useful model organism for examining these interactions. The ecological importance of copepods lies in their consumption of microzooplankton and phytoplankton as well as being prey in early life stages of fish species (Heneghan et al., 2016). The seasonal changes in lake temperature help to dictate the species diversity and abundance of copepods present in Lake Champlain. For the purpose of this study, three species were chosen, two within the same genus, to better understand how seasonality, temperature, and salinity interact to affect copepod populations: Leptodiaptomus minutus, L. sicilis and Skistodiaptomus spp.. L. minutus is a boreal species that appears primarily in mid to late autumn and again in early to mid spring (Torke, 2001). The counterpart to L. minutus is L. sicilis which appears primarily in the winter and early spring, and L. sicilis has been observed in a number of high saline lakes throughout the northern US and Canada for over 100 years (Hammer, 1993). Lake Champlain hosts two morphologically indistinguishable species: Skistodiaptomus pallidus and S. oregonensis. Both species are found in the summer months with S. oregonensis better adapted to eutrophic lakes than its counterpart (Torke, 2001). Our chosen calanoids are the most numerically dominant present in Lake Champlain making their responses help articulate larger trends in the lake. Sampling throughout different seasons not only allows for a larger breadth of variation to be incorporated, but also utilizes animals which have been exposed to varying levels of road salt runoff over the course of the year. While sampling, water samples were taken in order to assess lake levels of the ions being tested in the experiment. 

In this study, we investigate how road salts impact thermal limits of Skistodiaptomus spp. and two Leptodiaptomus copepod species. Salinity will be studied with the purpose of extrapolating the salt specific effects of major road salt components (NaCl and MgCl2) with the addition of a generalized road salt group. Copepods will be dosed at a range of salt concentrations and assessed for mortality over 5 days. After 5 days, the thermal maximum of a subset of copepods will be tested. Together, these results will provide insights to how human disturbances due to road salt impact fresh water communities.

# Methods

## Field Collections

Plankton were sampled at Lake Champlain in Burlington, VT, USA from September 2025 - March 2026 (coordinates: 44.481149, -73.225451). Sampling occurred using a 500 um mesh plankton net within the top 3-6 meters of the lake in a combination of horizontal and vertical tows. Surface water temperature was measured at the time of each sampling with a handheld thermometer and samples were placed in an insulated bag for transport back to the laboratory. In the laboratory, samples were dispersed in several 600mL beakers for storage and placed in a lab incubator (ThermoFisher Scientific Incubator, Model: TFFU20F2QWA). The incubator was adjusted to be within 5°C of the temperature recorded in the lake at the time each sample was taken. Continued temperature measurements are made by a USGS probe approximately 650 meters from the sampling site (coordinates: 44.47616017, -73.2215166) allowing for further analysis of our accuracy in lab to lake temperature shifts. Collection temperatures closely matched temperatures seen by the probe. During the sampling period of (1/27/26 - 3/23/26) Lake Champlain had frozen over making the primary sampling location inaccessible. Instead, a secondary location was chosen closer to shore with shallower water and a nearby marina kept the water moving to avoid freezing. Any samples taken during this time were from the secondary location.

## Copepod Identification and Experimental Set Up

Seasonality and species abundance was used to divide the project into two distinct groups: Fall sampling (L. minutus and Skistodiaptomus sp) and Winter sampling (L. sicilis). Lake Champlain has begun to see two distinct size morphs within a year of L. sicilis with body size differences instead of a singular morph similar to that of other calanoid species in the lake (Sasaki et al., In Review). Sampling for this experiment contained only one size morph for L. sicilis and body size measurements following heat testing were taken in order to ensure the same size morph was being used (Fig. 1). <!--# Body Size Figure Here -->

Our sampling from early fall through winter yielded survivorship data on three species of calanoid copepod in Lake Champlain. Identification remains uncertain with Skistodiaptomus as there are two species, S. oregonensis and S. pallidus which can only be distinguished through genetic methods. Historically, S. oregonensis has been identified within Lake Champlain (LaMay et al., 2013), but S. pallidus has also been found using genetic methods in surveys of the lake (Sasaki et al., In Review). Therefore, for the following project we acknowledge there is most likely a combination of the two species in our sample and refer to them as Skistodiaptomus spp.

Fresh plankton samples were used to complete each assay. When sorting through the bulk tow, calandoid copepods were isolated, identified to species, and adult females were selected for each species. Copepods in life stage C5 or C6 were classified as adults due to challenges in morphologically differentiating two with the understanding that the likelihood of a C5 animal ending up in a dish was randomized across all dishes.

Dose ranges were determined through previous pilot study and were adjusted over the course of the experiment to locate a range inducing 0-100% mortality. Both species demonstrated variation in their salt tolerance such that doses had to be adjusted regularly. This variation explains why the dose range of certain groups does not reach full mortality. Testing of these ranges consistently before animals were no longer available in the lake was a challenge. Treatment groups were replicated within each species for survivorship and thermal limits.

## Surviviorship Assays

Selected copepods were placed in petri dishes of 10mL spring water cooled to the collection temperature of the samples with 5 animals per dish. Each assay consisted of 10 total dishes: 2 control dishes of 20mL spring water and 8 treatment dishes with a combination of 10mL spring water and 10mL salt solution (Fig. 2). Salt solution is created through serial dilution across a selected range and is made at double the test dose to compensate for the 10mL spring water the copepods were sorted into. Each replication of a given salt group occurs with a new plankton tow sample. Treatment groups consist of NaCl and MgCl2 6H2O (henceforth referred to as MgCl2) (Fig. S1) with dose ranges selected with the goal of reaching 0-100% mortality in each range. In both salts Skistodiaptomus spp. were tested from 0.425-0.8 g/L with additional testing in NaCl at 1-1.2g/L, L. minutus was tested from 1-1.7g/L, and L. sicilis was tested from 1.2-2.6 g/L. Sample size differed between treatments and species due to varied copepod abundance levels and pilot treatments occurring in NaCl (Table 1). Copepods were acclimated to their given dose over the course of an hour with 10mL total of salt solution added. Dishes sat for 10 minutes following acclimation and survivorship was evaluated at "Hour 0". Sample dishes were kept at or near lake temperature for the entirety of the assay with survivorship being evaluated every 24 hours for 5 days. Survivorship was evaluated by gently disturbing the water inside the petri dish and watching for movement. If no movement was observed after a minute of observation and gentle movement of the water, the copepod was determined to have died. <!--# Graphical Methods Figure --> <!--# Sample Size Table -->

## Temperature Assays

Thermal limits were determined as critical thermal maximum measurements (CTmax) which identifies the temperature an individual no longer responds to stimuli in accordance with a previously developed procedure (Sasaki et al., 2023). The system utilizes two aquarium pumps, a reservoir containing a heating element, a plexiglass water bath, and a temperature probe. The aquarium pumps work in tandem with one circulating water within the reservoir and the other pumping water up into the water bath at which the samples sit. The water bath contains the temperature probe and a built-in test tube rack which holds the flat-bottom glass vials as they are tested. Temperature was recorded from the probe every 5 minutes over the course of the ramp. To begin, the system was lowered to the temperature at which the animals were being kept in the lab which remained near their collection temperature from the lake. Tubes were prepared with 10mL of the concentration of salt and spring water at which each sample was acclimated to and placed in the water bath to cool before animals were added. Animals selected from completed survivorship assays with mixed mortality were heat tested. These animals needed to have demonstrated a degree of movement prior to entering the assay due to the use of "ecological death" as an indicator as opposed to physiological death. Doses were randomly assigned throughout the rack. Once all animals were added, copepods were given a 10 minute resting period prior to the start of the temperature ramp. Any individuals who did not appear active after this resting period were removed from the assay. The temperature ramp began at approximately 0.3°C per minute and gradually decreased to approximately 0.1°C. Individuals were monitored throughout the assay until a response to stimulus was no longer observed (gentle turning of vials). At this time, the temperature was recorded as well as the time of removal. Once all individuals reached their thermal limit, animals were transferred to the lid of a 96 well plate and examined using a stereoscope (Olympus SZX7). Each individual was photographed to measure prosome length along with a scale micrometer. Measurements occurred in ImageJ (Schindelin et al., 2012).

## Water Testing

Water testing was completed using an Agilent 5800 ICP-OES device for metal ions (Na+, Mg2+). Water samples were taken at the time of each tow and were tested in bulk at the end of the experiment. Samples were filtered using grade 41 ashless filter paper prior to testing in the ICP-OES. A 12 point calibration curve (0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 13, 16, 20, 25, 30, 50, 100 ppm) was used with Na and Mg standards for ICP-OES (Fig. S1). The calibration curve contained three replicates of each point with two washes of 15% nitric acid and a blank in between each replication. Once established, samples were tested in succession with 10 replications of each measurement within the machine. After completion, intensity measurements were converted into concentrations of milligrams per liter for analysis.

## Statistical Analysis

All analyses were completed in R version 4.1.3 (Team, 2022). Survival curves were modeled as a logistic regression using a generalized linear mixed effects model with a binomial link function (Brooks et al., 2017). The data was converted from group survival data (the number of individuals surviving in each dish) to individual binary survival data (1 = survived, 0 = dead), with the correct number of 1s and 0s based on the group survival data. Additionally, we converted survivorship measurement times from hours since the experiment began to the nearest day. Binary survival data was then modeled as a function of fixed effects species, treatment (MgCl2 or NaCl), chloride concentration, and acclimation day, with a random intercept for each collection date. We then used a Type III ANOVA to identify significant effects.

Additionally, we examined how the chloride concentration inducing 50% mortality (LC50) changed over time during the experiments. We subset the data for each species, treatment, and day and then fit a logistic regression to each subset. Using these regressions, we estimated the LC50 as the concentration with a 50% probability of mortality using the dose.p function in the MASS package (Venables & Ripley, 2002).

We also used a linear mixed effects model to examine how salt-acclimation affected CTmax. Prior to analyses, data was filtered to exclude any copepods which were not actively swimming at temperatures below 15°C. We used a linear mixed effects model to examine how CTMax is affected by copepod species, treatment (MgCl2 or NaCl), and chloride concentration (with all interactions). Tube location within the CTmax machine and collection date were used as random intercepts. We checked assumptions using the performance package (Lüdecke et al., 2021). There was a low level of collinearity between X and Y, but all other assumptions were met. Using the linear mixed effects model, we then estimated the marginal trend of CTmax across chloride concentrations (e.g. the change in CTmax per gram added chloride) for each salt-species combination using the emmeans package (Lenth & Piaskowski, 2026).

# Results

## Survivorship

As chloride concentration increased, survivorship decreased over the course of 5-days for all species. When looking at the relationship between each species, we found changes in survivorship to be significant (p = 0.016). L. sicilis copepods were able to endure the highest chloride concentrations with L. minutus followed by Skistodiaptomus spp. seeing mortality at lower doses. In addition, depending on the treatment used (NaCl or MgCl2), we observed that an increase in chloride concentration had a significant impact on survivorship (p =0.010). For Skistodiaptomus spp., NaCl had a much stronger effect on survivorship than MgCl2. We observed a similar trend with L. minutus with NaCl having a stronger effect on mortality over 5 days than MgCl2. In contrast, for L. sicilis, we found MgCl2 had a stronger effect on mortality over 5 days than NaCl (Fig. 3). <!--# Survivorship matrix Figure -->

From the survivorship data, we fit a linear regression with values estimating LC50 by day between each group (Fig. 4). We observed more rapid effects of MgCl2 on both species than NaCl. Contrarily, copepods exposed to NaCl required a more prolonged exposure to high concentrations to reach an LC50 of ecologically relevant levels. Both groups reached a relatively stable LC50 value by the end of the 5-day experiment therefore we would not expect additional changes to survivorship in a longer experiment. <!--# lc50 Figure -->

## Thermal Tolerance

We used a linear mixed effects model to visualize the relationship between L. minutus and L. sicilis thermal limits and salt level as is standardized by chloride concentration. We did not see a discrete difference between collection temperature and CTmax value. Overall, we observed a difference in the effects of salinity on thermal limits between L. minutus and L. sicilis. NaCl and MgCl2 affected thermal limits of both species, but their relative effects varied. For L. minutus, NaCl had a slightly greater effect than MgCl2, whereas for L. sicilis, MgCl2 produced the strongest effect. Notably, in L. minutus, NaCl had a stronger effect than MgCl2 at the highest concentrations heat tested, even though NaCl was heat tested at a lower dose (Fig. 5). <!--# Linear mixed effects model -->

In L. minutus, both NaCl and MgCl2 did not have a significant effect on thermal limits. Whereas, in L. sicilis, increased salt concentrations had a significant effect on thermal limits (Fig. 6). Neither species had salt-specific trends for NaCl or MgCl2 in relation to CTmax. Notably, the salt group in each species which demonstrated higher mortality in the survivorship experiment also had a decreased trend in thermal limit within each species. These groups included NaCl in L. minutus and MgCl2 in L. sicilis. <!--# parameter estimate plot -->

We compared thermal limits to survival to confirm that observed differences in thermal tolerance were not driven by lower chloride levels within L. minutus. This visualization aims to create a standardized model of stress against the copepod. At LC50 in L. minutus, there were no salt-specific effects, though thermal limits decreased as mortality increased with increasing chloride concentration (Fig. 7). L. sicilis demonstrated a difference between NaCl and MgCl2 as mortality increased across doses with MgCl2 representing a much stronger effect on thermal limits as dose increased whereas NaCl had minimal effect on thermal limits as proportion mortality in dose groups increased. <!--# Proportion mortality plot -->

Throughout sampling, lake levels of Na and Mg ions sat comfortably below those tested in this experiment. Magnesium levels averaged at 4.21 mg/L and varied only slightly over the course of the experiment (min: 3.77 mg/L, max: 4.55 mg/L). Sodium levels averaged at 13.7 mg/L throughout the sampling period with moderately higher variation than seen in magnesium (min:12.67 mg/L, max:16.28 mg/L).

Upper doses of both MgCl2 and NaCl in L. sicilis also exhibited behavioral and physiological changes. Within the MgCl2 treatment, after 24 hours copepods had decreased movement with less "jumping" and instead only used much smaller movements to get around or waved their antennules which signaled their survivorship. The difference in movement patterns was stark. At lower doses there appeared to be no effect while in higher doses there was an extreme effect. At no middle dose was there a moderate effect. This reinforces the idea of thresholding in salinity tolerance for copepods and zooplankton as a whole. In NaCl groups, movement patterns were decreased, but not to the same degree as MgCl2. Copepods in the NaCl treatment tended to exhibit more movement and brushing of their antennules and with it more antenna damage and bending. MgCl2 as a whole had a much stronger effect on survivorship in L. sicilis than NaCl.

# Discussion

We observed variation in salt tolerance and thermal limits among both species of Leptodiaptomus copepods. By sampling over the course of 7 months we were able to observe seasonal differences in salinity and heat tolerance through different species of copepod. We hypothesized exposure to higher concentrations of NaCl and MgCl2 will increase mortality over a 5-day period, and we observed this to be correct in addition to salt specific effects being present in survivorship. Furthermore, we hypothesized copepods acclimated to higher salt concentrations would exhibit decreased thermal limits. We observed that as chloride concentration increased, L. sicilis thermal limits significantly decreased while there was no change in L. minutus. The difference of effects on thermal tolerance of these congeneric species contrasts the theory of phylogenetic conservatism which could be an interesting target for further research.

The application of road salt consists primarily of NaCl, but when pavement temperatures decrease to less than -9°C (16°F), MgCl2 is used to aid in breaking up ice on roads and sidewalks (Minnesota Pollution Control Agency, 2023). With a predicted increase in temperature oscillations throughout the winter months, we expect to see a higher number of acute warming events and therefore melting events in the deep winter (US Environmental Protection Agency, 2021). As we begin to see more runoff into the Lake Champlain basin, we would expect L. sicilis to be exposed to a greater proportion of MgCl2 than they had been previously. Additionally, as the experiment was standardized on chloride concentration, the levels of magnesium tested are half of those tested for sodium. With magnesium displaying an increasingly strong effect on survivorship, this indicates magnesium has a strong impact on physiology in copepods. With an increased sensitivity to MgCl2, L. sicilis may be at risk of acute mortality events or population weakening. Based on the findings of this study, MgCl2 as a de-icer poses a larger risk to winter copepod populations. This project suggests that management of MgCl2 salt use and minimization of MgCl2 as a de-icer at a policy level may help protect zooplankton communities in the long run.

Conversely, when looking at salt specific trends in L. minutus, we see no apparent impacts of MgCl2 on the copepods' thermal limits. This could mean a number of things such as adaptation to higher levels of MgCl2 due to L. minutus being present in the fall in which there are a higher number of temperature oscillating events. Similarly, L. minutus may be exposed to a lower concentration of MgCl2 in general as the low temperatures required for the use of this salt occur less frequently in the fall when L. minutus is present in the water than its counterpart L. sicilis in the winter. When examining salt specific effects more closely, L. minutus had no significant salt specific effects in thermal limits, but NaCl impacted survivorship and thermal limits slightly more than MgCl2. With continued applications of road salt and increased melting events, this sensitivity may pose a risk to populations under future conditions.

<!--# Merge this here from introduction: While calanoids are present throughout a variety of freshwater and marine conditions, L. sicilis has been observed in permanent mountain lakes, saline prairies, and shallow waters with a wide variety of temperature conditions though primarily acting as a winter species (Anderson, 1974). With the presence of L. siclilis in a multitude of saline lakes, higher salt tolerance levels were expected in the species than even those observed in these 62-6213 mg/L salinity lakes (Anderson, 1974), levels that exceed those tested in this experiment. -->

Not only does salinity impact survivorship, but salinity has the ability to impact physiologies of freshwater crustaceans and the molecular processes of many species. While our results found a significant effect of salt exposure on thermal limits in L. sicilis, the underlying cause of this trend remains uncertain. In copepods present in estuaries, exposure to high salinity has found changes in protein patterns within the animals (Gonzalez & Bradley, 1995). Additionally, modifications of proteins are thorough enough when exposed to these stressors that the variation in expression can be a distinguishable indicator of toxic salt exposures and heat stress (Gonzalez & Bradley, 1995). In Daphnia, heat shock proteins HSP 60, 70 and 90 were observed to increase in concentration following exposure to salt stress (Werner & Hinton, 2000). While these same proteins are found in copepods, it is unknown if the protein modifications observed in copepods are due to HSP proteins or another physiological pathway. Changes in salinity have also been observed to impact egg production and molting in fellow Leptodiaptomus copepod species suggesting the physiological changes we observed may be one of many effects on these individuals (Montiel-Martínez et al., 2008). In addition, a cross tolerance of NaCl to Ca2+ has been observed with this interaction suggesting an adaptation to NaCl may involve the Ca2+ metabolism (Zhao et al., 2023). As CaCl2 is another prominent de-icer, this interaction can inform further work into the cross tolerance of various de-icers themselves. In copepods, exposure to increased salt concentrations changed protein patterns and successive heat stress further modified the patterns (Gonzalez & Bradley, 1995). Therefore, further work must be done to understand the underlying mechanisms behind the physiological interaction of salt and heat stress.

Throughout the length of the experiment, we observed a wide variation in dose ranges necessary to create survivorship curves of each species. Dose ranges changed frequently in order to accommodate the species. This variation was yet another example of the thresholding present in salinity tolerance for zooplankton with varied mortality only being exhibited in a small range before a large die off event occurs. These trends indicate an increased potential for acute die off events as salinity levels continue to increase in lakes and fluctuate over time. The variation present does not appear to be connected to collection temperature or ion levels currently present in the lake, therefore further study would be required to understand the motivations behind such drastic changes in the populations. Sample variation described the primary limitation of our study. Notably, even with the amount of background variation present within the samples, we still observed distinct trends within the data. To understand this background variation, lab acclimated copepods could be used to test salt interactions while controlling for variables such as food availability throughout the year and other lake conditions.

As freshwater lakes continue to increase in salinity (Dugan et al. 2017), these populations may be at risk of decline. Without proper management, salinity will continue to compound in Lake Champlain (Kaushal et al. 2005) and threaten not only copepods but freshwater populations as a whole. Increased salinity by road salt application has reduced ecosystem function as well as decreased ecosystem services within these lakes (Kaushal et al. 2005) and changes in community composition (Kefford et al., 2016). With many freshwater species unable to contend with increasing salinity, freshwater systems will be expected to see a loss in biodiversity and abundance (Kefford et al., 2016) with long term impacts on community structure (Herbert et al., 2015). Increases in salinity and temperature in freshwater ecosystems are of growing concern and understanding the interaction of environmental stressors is crucial in predicting how ecosystems respond to climate change.
